sentences.text: Utahraptor is the only genus in its group and stands as the largest known member of the family Dromaeosauridae.
This massive predator measured approximately 6 to 7 meters in length and weighed around 500 kilograms.
Researchers in 1993 estimated that the premaxilla of Utahraptor was approximately 250% larger than that of Deinonychus.
The second toe claw of the holotype measured 22 cm along its curve and is estimated to be 24 cm in total length.
Some of its largest bones were found to be slightly larger than those of Achillobator.
The largest described specimen, BYUVP 15465, is estimated to have reached 7 meters in length and nearly 500 kilograms in weight, comparable to a polar bear.
In 2018, a 10-year-old student named Kenyon Roberts successfully proposed Utahraptor as the Utah state dinosaur, a proposal approved by the Senate.
On May 23, 2025, the Visitor Center of Utahraptor State Park opened to the public, displaying a Utahraptor skeleton alongside other Dalton Wells dinosaur species.
In 2001, researchers discovered a fossil block weighing 9 tons in eastern Utah containing the bones of at least seven Utahraptor individuals.
The genus Utahraptor was described by James Kirkland, Robert Gaston, and Donald Burge in 1993.
The type species Utahraptor ostrommaysi was named in 1993 based on fossils found in the Cedar Mountain Formation of Utah.
The first Utahraptor specimens were discovered in 1975 by Jim Jensen in the Dalton Wells Quarry near Moab, Utah.
Utahraptor hunted ankylosaurs and iguanodonts in the Cedar Mountain Formation ecosystem.
Sauropods approximately 20 meters long may have been an important part of the Utahraptor diet.
Evidence suggests Utahraptor was an ambush predator, unlike other dromaeosaurs which were pursuit predators.
Utahraptor was likely slower than Deinonychus and Velociraptor but faster than sauropods, moving at a speed similar to contemporary iguanodonts.
Unlike lighter dromaeosaurids that used hands for balance while kicking, the heavy Utahraptor could likely kick without losing balance and use its hands to kill prey.

Researchers noted that due to its enormous size, Utahraptor was not as fast as Deinonychus and Velociraptor but would have had a speed similar to contemporary iguanodontians and faster than sauropods.
If proven, group hunting by Utahraptors measuring at least 3.5 meters and weighing 70 kg could have killed prey up to 8 meters long and weighing 1 to 2 tons.
Fossil evidence suggests Utahraptor was social and practiced some form of post-nestling care.
The fossil block contained remains of at least seven Utahraptor individuals, including an adult approximately 4.8 meters long, four juveniles, and a hatchling about 1 meter long.
In a 2001 study by Bruce Rothschild and other paleontologists, two Utahraptor foot bones were examined for stress fractures, but none were found.
Utahraptor is classified as a large dromaeosaurid dinosaur, a group of feathered carnivorous theropods.
Utahraptor belongs to the family Dromaeosauridae, a group of theropod dinosaurs commonly called raptors.
Utahraptor lived during the Early Cretaceous period, specifically from the Berriasian to the Valanginian stages, with a possible record extending into the Hauterivian–Barremian stages.
Utahraptor lived between 139 and 134 million years ago during the Early Cretaceous in what is now North America.
Utahraptor was a major carnivore in the Early Cretaceous Arches region capable of attacking prey larger than itself.
In 2019, Costa and David criticized the emended name ostrommaysorum, arguing it lacks clear justification.
A 2019 analysis suggested Utahraptor might belong to a clade outside Dromaeosaurinae, though it could be reclassified into Dromaeosaurinae or Velociraptorinae with minor changes.
It is unclear whether all Utahraptor individuals in the fossil block became trapped simultaneously or were drawn in one by one.
